Mitosis 3D Lab

You started as a single cell. Today you are trillions, and your body makes billions more every day to heal cuts and replace worn-out cells. Use a microscope to catch onion root cells in the act of dividing, then step inside one cell to watch the chromosomes being copied and shared out. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🔁 The cell cycle

Interphase (G1 → S → G2) → Mitosis (P → M → A → T) → Cytokinesis

In S phase all the DNA is copied. In mitosis the copies are shared out. In cytokinesis the cell splits in two.

🎯 The big idea

1 cell → 2 cells with identical DNA

Mitosis lets a body grow and repair itself while every cell keeps the same full set of instructions. Checkpoints stop cells that are not ready.

Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file for grades 9–12 biology. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks and iPads included). Nothing is uploaded; results are saved in the browser on that device only, and students can download their data as a CSV file.

Learning goals

Students will be able to:

  • Set up and focus a compound light microscope, and calculate total magnification and field of view.
  • Identify interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase in onion root tip cells.
  • Calculate a mitotic index and estimate the time spent in each phase from cell counts.
  • Use a model to describe what happens to the chromosomes and the amount of DNA through the cell cycle.
  • Explain how checkpoint failures can lead to cells with the wrong chromosomes, and to cancer.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 · Onion Root Tip (1 period): Microscope skills (total magnification, field of view, image inversion), then cell counts on a stained onion root tip at 400×. Students count three fields in the zone of cell division and one farther back, then calculate the mitotic index and the time spent in each phase.
  • Lab 2 · Inside a Dividing Cell (½–1 period): The cell cycle in a 3D model cell with 4 chromosomes; DNA amount through the cycle; animal vs plant cytokinesis; checkpoints, nondisjunction and the link to cancer; Name That Phase quiz.

What the models assume

  • Lab 1: the slide is generated, not a photograph. About 22% of cells in the zone of cell division are in mitosis (roughly half of those in prophase), which is in the range students get from real onion root tips. Cells are drawn 30 µm wide. The cell cycle is taken as 24 hours; real onion root cells take roughly 16–24 hours depending on temperature.
  • Field of view values (4.5 mm, 1.8 mm, 0.45 mm) are typical for a school microscope with a 10× eyepiece. Your microscopes may differ slightly.
  • Lab 2 is not to scale and uses 2n = 4. Prometaphase is folded into prophase and metaphase, as in most high school texts. Checkpoint failures are shown one at a time; real cancers involve several mutations.

Misconceptions these labs target

  • “Interphase is a “resting” phase.” Lab 2 shows growth and DNA replication during interphase; Lab 1 shows most cells are in it because it lasts longest.
  • “Chromosomes are copied during prophase.” The DNA graph in Lab 2 rises in S phase, before chromosomes become visible.
  • “Daughter cells have half the chromosomes of the parent.” Students count 4 chromosomes in each daughter cell and contrast this with meiosis.
  • “Dividing cells are found all along a root.” A field counted farther from the tip has a mitotic index near zero.
  • “A microscope shows the specimen the same way up.” The letter “e” slide shows the image upside down and backward.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-4 (Use a model to illustrate the role of cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation in producing and maintaining complex organisms.). Practices: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking. Crosscutting concepts: Systems and System Models; Scale, Proportion, and Quantity.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42, adopted 2021): B.6A (explain the importance of the cell cycle to the growth of organisms, including the stages of the cell cycle and DNA replication); B.6C (relate disruptions of the cell cycle to the development of diseases such as cancer). Scientific and engineering practices: B.1D, B.1E, B.1F, B.1G, B.2C.
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments and taking measurements); RST.9-10.7 (translate information between words, tables, graphs and equations); HSN-Q.A.1 (use units to understand problems and guide multistep solutions; choose and interpret scales in graphs).
  • AP Biology (2025 course framework): 4.5 Cell Cycle; 4.6 Regulation of Cell Cycle.

Safety and risk assessment

Using the simulation (screen only: no chemicals or equipment)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Screen useEye strain, poor postureEach lab fits one class period. Build in a short break; look away from the screen every 20 minutes.
Flashing or moving imagesPhotosensitivity, motion discomfortNo flashing or strobing content. The 3D camera moves only when the student moves it; fly-through moves become instant jumps when the device is set to reduce motion.
Student dataPrivacyRuns offline. No accounts, no tracking and nothing uploaded. Results stay in the browser on that device and can be cleared at any time.

Onion root tip slides and microscope work (optional hands-on version of Lab 1)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Glass slides and coverslipsCutsPrepared slides are the safest option. Report breakages; sweep up with a brush and dustpan into a broken-glass container.
Stains (aceto-orcein, acetocarmine, toluidine blue)Stain skin and clothes; acetic acid stains are corrosive and irritate eyes and lungsSplash goggles, gloves and aprons; good ventilation; teacher dispenses small volumes.
Hydrochloric acid (1 M) used to soften root tipsCorrosive to eyes and skinTeacher only, or use prepared slides.
MicroscopesDropped equipment; hot lamp; damage to slide and lensCarry with two hands (arm and base). Start on the lowest power. Never use the coarse focus on high power. Never use direct sunlight as the light source.
Electrical cordsTrips, shockKeep cords tidy and away from sinks.

This table supports, but does not replace, your own school or district risk assessment. Follow your chemical hygiene plan, read the SDS for every chemical, and check state and district rules before any hands-on activity.

Sensitive content

  • Cancer is discussed as a failure of cell-cycle control. Some students will have family experience of it. Keep the discussion factual.

Accessibility

  • In the cell count, click the eyepiece image, then use the arrow keys to move between cells and the keys I, P, M, A, T to mark them. A text description of each selected cell is announced to screen readers.
  • Phases are marked with letters as well as colors.
  • All controls work with the keyboard: Tab to move, Enter or Space to press, arrow keys on sliders. In the 3D view, arrow keys rotate and the + and − keys zoom.
  • Gray controls cannot be used yet. They stay reachable and explain why when pressed.
  • Nothing is shown by color alone: right and wrong answers are marked ✓ and ✗, and results are given in words and numbers.
  • No sound, no flashing content, and no time limits that cannot be repeated. Text stays readable when the browser is zoomed to 200%.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan.
